claim: The Drosophila Heterochromatin Protein 1 (HP1) variant Rhino permits transcription of PIWI-interacting RNA (piRNA) precursors within transposon-rich heterochromatic loci in germline cells.
source: The Drosophila Heterochromatin Protein 1 (HP1) variant Rhino permits transcription of PIWI-interacting RNA (piRNA) precursors within transposon-rich heterochromatic loci in germline cells.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about Rhino's function supported by the manuscript's experimental data and cited literature.

claim: Current models propose that Rhino's specific chromatin occupancy at piRNA source loci is determined by histone marks and maternally inherited piRNAs.
source: Current models propose that Rhino's specific chromatin occupancy at piRNA source loci is determined by histone marks and maternally inherited piRNAs, but also imply the existence of other, undiscovered specificity cues.
evidence: This statement references existing models in the field, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Kipferl is a member of the diverse family of zinc finger associated domain (ZAD)-C2H2 zinc finger proteins.
source: Here, we identify a member of the diverse family of zinc finger associated domain (ZAD)-C2H2 zinc finger proteins, Kipferl, as critical Rhino cofactor in ovaries.
evidence: The protein domain architecture is shown in Figure 2A and confirmed through sequence analysis.

claim: Kipferl binds to guanosine-rich DNA motifs.
source: By binding to guanosine-rich DNA motifs and interacting with the Rhino chromodomain, Kipferl recruits Rhino to specific loci and stabilizes it on chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 5I and ChIP-seq data in Figure 5J.

claim: Kipferl interacts with the Rhino chromodomain.
source: By binding to guanosine-rich DNA motifs and interacting with the Rhino chromodomain, Kipferl recruits Rhino to specific loci and stabilizes it on chromatin.
evidence: This is demonstrated through yeast two-hybrid experiments shown in Figure 6H and supported by genetic data.

claim: In kipferl mutant flies, Rhino is lost from most of its target chromatin loci.
source: In kipferl mutant flies, Rhino is lost from most of its target chromatin loci and instead accumulates on pericentromeric Satellite arrays, resulting in decreased levels of transposon targeting piRNAs and impaired fertility.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq data in Figure 3D-E and quantified in Figure 3E.

claim: In kipferl mutant flies, Rhino accumulates on pericentromeric Satellite arrays.
source: In kipferl mutant flies, Rhino is lost from most of its target chromatin loci and instead accumulates on pericentromeric Satellite arrays, resulting in decreased levels of transposon targeting piRNAs and impaired fertility.
evidence: This is shown by ChIP-seq data in Figure 3I and RNA FISH in Figure 3J.

claim: kipferl mutant flies show decreased levels of transposon targeting piRNAs.
source: In kipferl mutant flies, Rhino is lost from most of its target chromatin loci and instead accumulates on pericentromeric Satellite arrays, resulting in decreased levels of transposon targeting piRNAs and impaired fertility.
evidence: This is demonstrated by small RNA-seq data in Figure 4C-D.

claim: kipferl mutant flies have impaired fertility.
source: In kipferl mutant flies, Rhino is lost from most of its target chromatin loci and instead accumulates on pericentromeric Satellite arrays, resulting in decreased levels of transposon targeting piRNAs and impaired fertility.
evidence: This is shown by hatching rate experiments in Figure 3B.

claim: DNA sequence, in addition to the H3K9me3 mark, determines the identity of piRNA source loci.
source: Our findings reveal that DNA sequence, in addition to the H3K9me3 mark, determines the identity of piRNA source loci and provide insight into how Rhino might be caught in the crossfire of genetic conflicts.
evidence: This is supported by the demonstration that Kipferl binds specific DNA motifs and is required for Rhino localization.

claim: Loss of the piRNA pathway leads to transposon de-repression and mobilization, DNA damage, and sterility.
source: Its loss leads to transposon de-repression and mobilization, DNA damage, and sterility.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by the citations provided (Siomi et al., 2011; Czech et al., 2018; Ozata et al., 2019, Senti and Brennecke, 2010).

claim: PIWI clade Argonaute proteins are loaded with 23-30nt long piRNAs.
source: At the center of the piRNA pathway are Argonaute proteins of the PIWI clade loaded with 23-30nt long piRNAs which enable sequence specific repression of transposons at the transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels.
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of the piRNA pathway.

claim: piRNAs enable sequence specific repression of transposons at the transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels.
source: At the center of the piRNA pathway are Argonaute proteins of the PIWI clade loaded with 23-30nt long piRNAs which enable sequence specific repression of transposons at the transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels.
evidence: This is a fundamental mechanism of the piRNA pathway.

claim: Transposon targeting piRNAs are typically encoded in specialized genomic regions called piRNA clusters.
source: Transposon targeting piRNAs are typically encoded in specialized genomic regions (Brennecke et al., 2007; Houwing et al., 2007; Aravin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and is a foundational concept in piRNA biology.

claim: piRNA clusters are enriched in transposon sequences.
source: These so-called piRNA clusters are enriched in transposon sequences, range from a few to several hundred kilobases in length, and act as heritable and adaptive transposon sequence libraries for the piRNA pathway.
evidence: This is a well-documented characteristic of piRNA clusters.

claim: piRNA clusters range from a few to several hundred kilobases in length.
source: These so-called piRNA clusters are enriched in transposon sequences, range from a few to several hundred kilobases in length, and act as heritable and adaptive transposon sequence libraries for the piRNA pathway.
evidence: This is a documented characteristic of piRNA clusters.

claim: piRNA clusters act as heritable and adaptive transposon sequence libraries for the piRNA pathway.
source: These so-called piRNA clusters are enriched in transposon sequences, range from a few to several hundred kilobases in length, and act as heritable and adaptive transposon sequence libraries for the piRNA pathway.
evidence: This is a conceptual understanding of piRNA cluster function.

claim: In Drosophila gonads, two general types of piRNA clusters are distinguished based on their mode of transcription: Uni-strand clusters and dual-strand piRNA clusters.
source: In Drosophila gonads, two general types of piRNA clusters are distinguished based on their mode of transcription: Uni-strand clusters are transcribed on one genomic strand from canonical RNA polymerase II promoters, giving rise to long, single stranded, and poly-adenylated transcripts (Brennecke et al., 2007; Mohn et al., 2014; Goriaux et al., 2014). The second type are dual-strand piRNA clusters, which are transcribed on both genomic strands (Brennecke et al., 2007; Mohn et al., 2014; Klattenhoff et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2014b; Chen et al., 2016; Andersen et al., 2017).
evidence: This classification is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Uni-strand clusters are transcribed on one genomic strand from canonical RNA polymerase II promoters, giving rise to long, single stranded, and poly-adenylated transcripts.
source: Uni-strand clusters are transcribed on one genomic strand from canonical RNA polymerase II promoters, giving rise to long, single stranded, and poly-adenylated transcripts (Brennecke et al., 2007; Mohn et al., 2014; Goriaux et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Dual-strand piRNA clusters are transcribed on both genomic strands.
source: The second type are dual-strand piRNA clusters, which are transcribed on both genomic strands (Brennecke et al., 2007; Mohn et al., 2014; Klattenhoff et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2014b; Chen et al., 2016; Andersen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Dual-strand clusters are active in germline cells and are embedded within heterochromatin.
source: Dual-strand clusters are active in germline cells and are embedded within heterochromatin.
evidence: This is a documented characteristic of dual-strand clusters.

claim: Dual-strand clusters differ from canonical RNA polymerase II transcription units by a lack of defined promoters, and by suppression of splicing and cleavage- and polyadenylation signals.
source: They differ from canonical RNA polymerase II transcription units by a lack of defined promoters, and by suppression of splicing and cleavage- and polyadenylation signals.
evidence: This is a documented characteristic of dual-strand clusters.

claim: The molecular identity of dual-strand piRNA clusters is conferred by Rhino, a germline-specific variant of the canonical Heterochromatin Protein 1 a (Su(var)2–5).
source: The molecular identity of dual-strand piRNA clusters is conferred by Rhino, a germline-specific variant of the canonical Heterochromatin Protein 1 a (Su(var)2–5) (Vermaak and Malik, 2009; Klattenhoff et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Su(var)2–5 mediates gene silencing and chromatin compaction.
source: While Su(var)2–5 mediates gene silencing and chromatin compaction, Rhino acts in an opposite manner
evidence: This is a well-established function of HP1a.

claim: Rhino enables the recruitment of several germline-specific proteins required to engage the cellular gene expression machinery at piRNA clusters and enable the nuclear export of the emerging transcripts.
source: It enables the recruitment of several germline-specific proteins, which are required to engage the cellular gene expression machinery at piRNA clusters and enable the nuclear export of the emerging transcripts (ElMaghraby et al., 2019; Andersen et al., 2017; Mohn et al., 2014; Kneuss et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2014b; Zhang et al., 2012a; Zhang et al., 2018; Hur et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In rhino mutant flies, dual-strand piRNA clusters lose their transcriptional capacity and convert into canonical heterochromatin.
source: In rhino mutant flies, dual-strand piRNA clusters lose their transcriptional capacity and convert into canonical heterochromatin.
evidence: This is a documented phenotype of rhino mutants.

claim: In rhino mutant flies, piRNA production collapses, transposons are de-repressed, and flies are sterile.
source: Consequently, piRNA production collapses, transposons are de-repressed, and flies are sterile.
evidence: This is a documented phenotype of rhino mutants.

claim: Rhino is the defining feature of dual-strand piRNA clusters.
source: Based on these data, Rhino is the defining feature of dual-strand piRNA clusters, and its specific deposition is at the very center of steering piRNA populations to target 'non-self' (transposons) but not 'self' (genic loci).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cited literature and experimental data.

claim: Current models involve a role of maternally inherited Piwi-piRNA complexes in the specification of piRNA cluster identity through Piwi-dependent deposition of H3K9 methylation.
source: Current models involve a role of maternally inherited Piwi-piRNA complexes in the specification of piRNA cluster identity through Piwi-dependent deposition of H3K9 methylation, which is postulated to define dual-strand clusters at the chromatin level (Mohn et al., 2014; Le Thomas et al., 2014; Shpiz et al., 2014; Akkouche et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Rhino's N-terminal chromodomain displays specific affinity to H3K9me3.
source: Indeed, Rhino's N-terminal chromodomain displays specific affinity to H3K9me3, which is consistently present at piRNA clusters (Mohn et al., 2014; Le Thomas et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: A large fraction of the pericentromeric, H3K9me3 enriched heterochromatin is not or only weakly bound by Rhino.
source: However, a large fraction of the pericentromeric, H3K9me3 enriched heterochromatin is not or only weakly bound by Rhino.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the ChIP-seq data in Figure 1E-F.

claim: While Rhino is expressed both in ovaries and testes, the identity of dual-strand piRNA clusters differs in the two gonads despite identical DNA sequence.
source: First, while Rhino is expressed both in ovaries and testes, the identity of dual-strand piRNA clusters differs in the two gonads despite identical DNA sequence (Mohn et al., 2014; Klattenhoff et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: The genomic Rhino profile is dynamic in testes where the X-chromosomal AT-chX cluster attracts most of the cellular Rhino pool in differentiating spermatocytes but not at earlier developmental stages.
source: Moreover, the genomic Rhino profile is dynamic in testes where the X-chromosomal AT-chX cluster attracts most of the cellular Rhino pool in differentiating spermatocytes but not at earlier developmental stages (Chen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Only around 20% of the insertions of any given transposon are bound by Rhino.
source: Second, while all stand-alone insertions of active transposons are silenced through piRNA-guided heterochromatin formation, only around 20% of the insertions of any given transposon are, by unknown mechanisms, bound by Rhino (Mohn et al., 2014; Shpiz et al., 2014; Radion et al., 2019, Akulenko et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: The zinc finger protein CG2678/Kipferl defines the majority of Rhino's chromatin binding pattern in ovaries.
source: Here, we show that the zinc finger protein CG2678/Kipferl defines the majority of Rhino's chromatin binding pattern in ovaries.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the ChIP-seq data in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: The combinatorial readout of Kipferl's sequence-specific DNA binding together with Rhino's affinity to the H3K9me3 mark underlies the selective recognition of heterochromatic loci as substrates for piRNA precursor transcription.
source: The combinatorial readout of Kipferl's sequence-specific DNA binding together with Rhino's affinity to the H3K9me3 mark underlies the selective recognition of heterochromatic loci as substrates for piRNA precursor transcription.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A substantial fraction of the genome (3.9 Mbp corresponding to ~3% of the analyzable genome in the w1118 strain) showed greater than 4-fold enrichment for Rhino over input.
source: This revealed that a substantial fraction of the genome (e.g. 3.9 Mbp corresponding to ~3% of the analyzable genome in the w1118 strain) showed greater than 4-fold enrichment (p<0.036, Z-score >2.1) for Rhino over input.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the ChIP-seq analysis.

claim: Rhino enrichment at major dual-strand clusters and within the recombination-poor, pericentromeric heterochromatin followed a highly similar pattern in all three fly strains (w1118, MTD-Gal4, and iso1).
source: Rhino enrichment at major dual-strand clusters but also within the recombination-poor, pericentromeric heterochromatin followed a highly similar pattern in all three fly strains, with only few loci displaying strain-specific quantitative differences (Figure 1B left, middle; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the scatter plots in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Many Rhino domains in pericentromeric heterochromatin exhibited strong H3K9me3 signal, gave rise to abundant piRNAs, and were enriched in diverse transposon sequences.
source: Many Rhino domains in pericentromeric heterochromatin (e.g. Figure 1C panel 1) resembled the large piRNA clusters like cluster 80F (Figure 1C panel 2): they exhibited strong H3K9me3 signal, gave rise to abundant piRNAs, and were enriched in diverse transposon sequences.
evidence: This is shown in the genome browser tracks in Figure 1C.

claim: Several strain-specific Rhino domains within chromosome arms corresponded to genomic loci flanking stand-alone transposon insertions.
source: Based on manual inspection, these corresponded to genomic loci flanking stand-alone transposon insertions (e.g. a flea insertion found only in the w1118 strain (Figure 1C panel 3)).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C panel 3.

claim: Many shared euchromatic Rhino domains were not associated with transposon insertions.
source: Based on the iso1 data and the reference genome, many of these shared domains were not associated with transposon insertions.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the iso1 strain data against the reference genome.

claim: The locus upstream of the headcase gene shows strong Rhino enrichment in all strains, although this locus lacks transposon sequences and does not produce abundant piRNAs.
source: Upstream of the headcase locus, for example, Rhino was strongly enriched in all strains, although this locus lacks transposon sequences and does not produce abundant piRNAs (Figure 1C panel 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C panel 4.

claim: Transposon-devoid Rhino loci display dual-strand transcription based on RIP-seq data for Nxf3.
source: Nonetheless, these loci displayed dual-strand transcription based on RIP-seq data for Nxf3 (ElMaghraby et al., 2019), the piRNA precursor specific nuclear export factor, indicating that these loci were functional Rhino domains (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and supported by the cited reference.

claim: The poor piRNA output from transposon-devoid loci is most likely due to a lack of piRNA target sites for Aub/Ago3-mediated transcript cleavage in the emerging transcripts, which greatly stimulate piRNA biogenesis.
source: The poor piRNA output from these transposon-devoid loci is therefore not due to non-functional Rhino, but most likely due to a lack of piRNA target sites for Aub/Ago3-mediated transcript cleavage in the emerging transcripts, which greatly stimulate piRNA biogenesis (Mohn et al., 2015; Han et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and supported by the cited references.

claim: Rhino, in a largely strain-independent manner, binds to thousands of remarkably diverse genomic loci that include, but are not limited to sources of dual-strand piRNAs.
source: Altogether, our data demonstrate that Rhino, in a largely strain-independent manner, binds to thousands of remarkably diverse genomic loci that include, but are not limited to sources of dual-strand piRNAs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the ChIP-seq analysis across multiple strains.

claim: Rhino domains in both pericentromeric heterochromatin and within chromosome arms consistently showed enrichment in H3K9me3.
source: Consistent with a reported role of H3K9 methylation in dual-strand piRNA cluster biology, Rhino domains in both pericentromeric heterochromatin and within chromosome arms consistently showed enrichment in H3K9me3 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown in the violin plots in Figure 1D.

claim: H3K9me3 levels do not directly correlate with Rhino enrichments.
source: However, H3K9me3 levels did not directly correlate with Rhino enrichments
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: Enrichments of H3K9me3 were considerably higher for Rhino domains within pericentromeric heterochromatin compared to those in chromosome arms, despite comparable Rhino enrichments.
source: First, enrichments of H3K9me3 were considerably higher for Rhino domains within pericentromeric heterochromatin compared to those in chromosome arms, despite comparable Rhino enrichments (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Numerous loci in heterochromatin with high H3K9me3 signal were not or only poorly bound by Rhino.
source: Second, numerous loci in heterochromatin with high H3K9me3 signal were not or only poorly bound by Rhino (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: The recombinant Rhino chromodomain binds to H3K9me2, yet with lower affinity than H3K9me3.
source: Besides H3K9me3, the recombinant Rhino chromodomain also binds to H3K9me2, yet with lower affinity (Mohn et al., 2014; Le Thomas et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: A large fraction of H3K9me2 was found outside of Rhino-bound loci.
source: As for H3K9me3, however, a large fraction of H3K9me2 was found outside of Rhino-bound loci (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Su(var)2–5 enrichments followed H3K9me2/3 levels at almost all genomic loci.
source: In contrast, Su(var)2–5 enrichments followed H3K9me2/3 levels at almost all genomic loci (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C compared to Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Methylation of H3K9 alone, while being a hallmark of Rhino domains, cannot explain Rhino's chromatin profile.
source: Thus, methylation of H3K9 alone, while being a hallmark of Rhino domains, cannot explain Rhino's chromatin profile.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ChIP-seq data comparing H3K9me2/3 and Rhino enrichments.

claim: CG2678 was the second most enriched hit in a yeast two-hybrid screen using full length Rhino as bait, with twelve independent clones.
source: With twelve independent clones, the uncharacterized protein CG2678 was the second most enriched screen hit.
evidence: This is a result from the yeast two-hybrid screen described in the methods.

claim: CG2678 encodes a predicted DNA binder whose two annotated protein isoforms carry one or two arrays of C2H2 zinc fingers.
source: CG2678 encodes a predicted DNA binder whose two annotated protein isoforms carry one or two arrays of C2H2 zinc fingers (ZnFs) (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CG2678 is a member of the large group of ZAD-ZnF proteins that have radiated extensively in insects based on an N-terminal ZnF associated domain (ZAD).
source: Based on an N-terminal ZnF associated domain (ZAD), CG2678 is a member of the large group of ZAD-ZnF proteins that have radiated extensively in insects (Chung et al., 2007; Chung et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on domain analysis and supported by the cited references.

claim: D. melanogaster has over 90 ZAD-ZnF proteins.
source: Only a handful of the >90 D. melanogaster ZAD-ZnF proteins have been studied
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the ZAD-ZnF protein family.

claim: Studied ZAD-ZnF proteins are involved in transcription, genome organization, and heterochromatin biology.
source: Only a handful of the >90 D. melanogaster ZAD-ZnF proteins have been studied, and these are involved in transcription (Bag et al., 2021; Harms et al., 2000), genome organization (Maksimenko et al., 2015; Sabirov et al., 2021), and heterochromatin biology (Kasinathan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: CG2678 was enriched in the Rhino-GFP TurboID sample versus a control sample at similar levels as the piRNA cluster factors Deadlock, Cutoff, and Bootlegger.
source: This revealed that CG2678 was enriched in the Rhino-GFP sample versus a control sample at similar levels as the piRNA cluster factors Deadlock, Cutoff, and Bootlegger (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown in the volcano plot in Figure 2B.

claim: CG2678 mRNA levels were detected primarily in ovaries.
source: Like for rhino, CG2678 mRNA levels were detected primarily in ovaries (Flybase gene expression atlas, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, Larkin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and supported by the cited reference.

claim: CG2678 is expressed specifically in ovarian germline cells, with no detectable signal above background in somatic cells.
source: Immunofluorescence experiments revealed CG2678 expression specifically in ovarian germline cells, with no detectable signal above background in somatic cells which lack Rhino-defined piRNA clusters (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in the immunofluorescence images in Figure 2C.

claim: In germline nurse cells, CG2678 was enriched in nuclei and accumulated in numerous discrete foci in a pattern that was almost indistinguishable from that of a Rhino staining.
source: In germline nurse cells, CG2678 was enriched in nuclei and accumulated in numerous discrete foci in a pattern that was almost indistinguishable from that of a Rhino staining (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Single cell RNA-seq data from adult ovaries indicated low CG2678 mRNA levels in germline stem cells and increased levels in differentiating nurse cells.
source: Single cell RNA-seq data from adult ovaries indicated low mRNA levels in germline stem cells and increased levels in differentiating nurse cells (Rust et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: CG2678 protein, while abundant in differentiating cysts and polyploid nurse cells, was barely detectable in germline stem cells and cystoblasts despite these cells expressing Rhino.
source: Consistent with this, CG2678 protein, while abundant in differentiating cysts and polyploid nurse cells, was barely detectable in germline stem cells and cystoblasts despite these cells expressing Rhino (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: CG2678 was not detectable in testes.
source: CG2678 was further not detectable in testes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: CG2678 co-occupied Rhino domains genome-wide in all three wild-type strains (w1118, MTD-Gal4, and iso1 strains).
source: ChIP-seq experiments using anti-CG2678 antibody confirmed that the co-localization of CG2678 and Rhino in nuclear foci was due to both proteins binding the same chromatin sites, as CG2678 co-occupied Rhino domains genome-wide in all three wild-type strains (w1118, MTD-Gal4, and iso1 strains) (Figure 2E; Figure 2—figure supplement 2D, E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D, E.

claim: CG2678 and Rhino bind to chromatin in a virtually indistinguishable pattern, often occupying broad chromatin domains.
source: Closer inspection revealed that CG2678 and Rhino bind to chromatin in a virtually indistinguishable pattern, often occupying broad chromatin domains.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the ChIP-seq data in Figure 2F.

claim: 647 genomic 1-kb tiles exhibited significantly higher enrichment for CG2678 than for Rhino (Z-score >3) and were not enriched for Rhino (CG2678-only loci; 15.4% of all Kipferl-bound tiles).
source: Notably, 647 genomic 1-kb tiles exhibited significantly higher enrichment for CG2678 than for Rhino (Z-score >3) and were not enriched for Rhino (CG2678-only loci; 15.4% of all Kipferl-bound tiles) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E.

claim: At CG2678-only loci, the CG2678 ChIP-seq signal formed narrow peaks.
source: At these loci, the CG2678 ChIP-seq signal formed narrow peaks (e.g. Figure 2G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2G.

claim: 98.7% of the CG2678-only loci resided within chromosome arms.
source: 98.7% of the CG2678-only loci resided within chromosome arms, suggesting that lack of H3K9 methylation at these sites might prevent stable Rhino binding.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the ChIP-seq analysis.

claim: Almost all CG2678-only loci were devoid of H3K9 methylation.
source: Indeed, almost all CG2678-only loci were devoid of H3K9 methylation (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: CG2678 null mutant flies were viable.
source: CG2678 null mutant flies were viable and, in western blot analysis, did not express detectable CG2678 protein (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CG2678 null mutant flies did not express detectable CG2678 protein.
source: CG2678 null mutant flies were viable and, in western blot analysis, did not express detectable CG2678 protein (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in the western blot in Figure 3A.

claim: CG2678 mutant females showed normal egg-laying rates but strong fertility defects.
source: CG2678 mutant females showed normal egg-laying rates but strong fertility defects (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Insertion of the CG2678 genomic sequence with an internal FLAG-tag at the deleted locus restored fertility to wildtype levels.
source: Insertion of the CG2678 genomic sequence with an internal FLAG-tag (Figure 2A) at the deleted locus restored fertility to wildtype levels (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Loss of CG2678 had no impact on Rhino levels.
source: Loss of CG2678 had no impact on Rhino levels (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is shown in the western blot in Figure 3A.

claim: Loss of CG2678 resulted in pronounced changes in Rhino localization: In wildtype nurse cells, Rhino accumulated in many distinct foci throughout the nucleus. In CG2678 mutants, almost all Rhino signal gathered in a few large, often continuous structures adjacent to the nuclear envelope.
source: Loss of CG2678 had no impact on Rhino levels (Figure 3A) but resulted in pronounced changes in Rhino localization: In wildtype nurse cells, Rhino accumulated in many distinct foci throughout the nucleus. In CG2678 mutants, almost all Rhino signal gathered in a few large, often continuous structures adjacent to the nuclear envelope (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in the confocal images in Figure 3C.

claim: Depletion of CG2678 mRNA by germline-specific RNAi caused a similar Rhino localization phenotype as CG2678 mutants.
source: Depletion of CG2678 mRNA by germline-specific RNAi caused a similar phenotype (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Expression of a tagged wildtype CG2678 protein in CG2678 mutants restored wildtype Rhino localization to small, dispersed foci.
source: and expression of a tagged wildtype CG2678 protein in CG2678 mutants restored wildtype Rhino localization to small, dispersed foci (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The prominent Rhino accumulations in CG2678 mutants were enriched in H3K9me3 and the Rhino co-factors Deadlock and Nxf3, indicating that they were genuine chromosomal Rhino domains.
source: The prominent Rhino accumulations in CG2678 mutants were enriched in H3K9me3 and the Rhino co-factors Deadlock and Nxf3, indicating that they were genuine chromosomal Rhino domains (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: In CG2678,nxf3 double mutant flies, Rhino still accumulated in few, large foci but these were no longer confined to the nuclear envelope.
source: Indeed, in CG2678,nxf3 double mutant flies, Rhino still accumulated in few, large foci but these were no longer confined to the nuclear envelope (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In the absence of Kipferl, Rhino's chromatin association was severely reduced at most genomic sites.
source: In the absence of Kipferl, Rhino's chromatin association was severely reduced at most genomic sites (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Rhino loss at various genomic loci in kipferl mutants was not caused by reduced H3K9 methylation levels, as H3K9me2/3 levels remained high at Rhino-bound regions upon depletion of Kipferl.
source: Importantly, Rhino loss at these various genomic loci was not caused by reduced H3K9 methylation levels, as H3K9me2/3 levels remained high at Rhino-bound regions upon depletion of Kipferl (Figure 3G; Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Only 4.6% of all 1-kb tiles exhibiting a more than fourfold Rhino enrichment in control flies remained Rhino-bound in kipferl-depleted ovaries.
source: Only 4.6% of all 1-kb tiles exhibiting a more than fourfold Rhino enrichment (n=2) in control flies remained Rhino-bound in kipferl-depleted ovaries.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the ChIP-seq analysis.

claim: Among the tiles that remained Rhino-bound in kipferl-depleted ovaries were mainly tiles of piRNA cluster 42AB and, to a lesser extent, cluster 38C.
source: Among these were mainly tiles of piRNA cluster 42AB and, to a lesser extent, cluster 38C (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) experiments confirmed that clusters 42AB and 38C are transcribed in kipferl mutants.
source: Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) experiments confirmed that clusters 42AB and 38C are transcribed in kipferl mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).

claim: The average Rhino enrichment on transposon consensus sequences varied between two and 30-fold in wildtype ovaries, was non-detectable in ovaries depleted for Rhino, and was strongly reduced in the absence of Kipferl.
source: Based on an analysis of all ChIP-seq reads, the average Rhino enrichment on transposon consensus sequences varied between two and 30-fold in wildtype ovaries, was non-detectable in ovaries depleted for Rhino, and was strongly reduced in the absence of Kipferl (Figure 3H).

claim: Several Satellite sequences, foremost the Responder and 1.688 family Satellites, maintained Rhino occupancy or accumulated even more Rhino than in wildtype ovaries in kipferl mutants.
source: In contrast, several Satellite sequences, foremost the Responder and 1.688 family Satellites that give rise to Rhino-dependent piRNAs in wildtype ovaries and testes (Chen et al., 2021; Wei et al., 2021), maintained Rhino occupancy or accumulated even more Rhino than in wildtype ovaries (Figure 3I).

claim: Consistent with elevated Rhino occupancy at Rsp and 1.688 Satellites in kipferl mutants, there was a corresponding increase in nascent transcripts as indicated by the enhanced RNA FISH signal in nurse cell nuclei.

claim: The FISH signal for Rsp and 1.688 transcripts in kipferl mutants overlapped precisely with the prominent Rhino accumulations at the nuclear envelope.
source: The FISH signal for Rsp and 1.688 transcripts in kipferl mutants overlapped precisely with the prominent Rhino accumulations at the nuclear envelope.

claim: The 359 bp array (1.688 family) on the X-chromosome extends over several megabasepairs.

evidence: This is stated as a fact about the satellite repeat and supported by literature.

claim: Total piRNA levels, normalized to miRNA reads, were reduced 4.5-fold in rhino-depleted but only 1.5-fold in kipferl-depleted ovaries.
source: Total piRNA levels, normalized to miRNA reads, were reduced 4.5-fold in rhino-depleted but only 1.5-fold in kipferl-depleted ovaries (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).

claim: kipferl-depleted ovaries exhibited reduced piRNA levels only from Rhino-dependent germline source loci.
source: kipferl-depleted ovaries exhibited reduced piRNA levels only from Rhino-dependent germline source loci (Figure 4A).

claim: At cluster 80F, piRNA production collapsed in the absence of Kipferl to the same extent as seen in rhino-depleted ovaries.
source: A prominent example was cluster 80F, where piRNA production collapsed in the absence of Kipferl to the same extent as seen in rhino-depleted ovaries (Figure 4A and B).

claim: At piRNA clusters 38C and 42AB, piRNA losses in kipferl-depleted ovaries were less severe compared to rhino-depleted ovaries, consistent with residual Rhino binding to both clusters.
source: At many other sites, piRNA losses were less severe compared to rhino-depleted ovaries. Among them were piRNA clusters 38C and 42AB, consistent with residual Rhino binding to both clusters in kipferl-depleted ovaries (Figure 4A and B; Figure 3D and E).

claim: The selective impact of kipferl depletion on germline-specific, Rhino-dependent piRNA source loci was reflected when piRNAs mapping in antisense orientation to transposon consensus sequences were analyzed.
source: The selective impact of kipferl depletion on germline-specific, Rhino-dependent piRNA source loci was also reflected when piRNAs mapping in antisense orientation to transposon consensus sequences were analyzed (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: piRNAs targeting soma-controlled transposons (e.g. Tabor, gypsy5, ZAM; mostly originating from flamenco) were not affected in rhino- or kipferl-depleted ovaries.
source: piRNAs targeting soma-controlled transposons (e.g. Tabor, gypsy5, ZAM; mostly originating from flamenco) were not affected in rhino- or kipferl-depleted ovaries.

claim: For most transposons with dominating germline piRNA populations that are targeted by Rhino-dependent piRNAs, piRNA pools were reduced in kipferl-depleted ovaries.

All other transposons were targeted by Rhino-dependent piRNAs. For most of these elements, piRNA pools were reduced in kipferl-depleted ovaries (Figure 4D left, E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: The few transposons that retained piRNAs or even displayed increased piRNA levels in kipferl-depleted ovaries had insertions in piRNA clusters 38C or 42AB, where Rhino binding was largely Kipferl-independent.
source: The few transposons that retained piRNAs or even displayed increased piRNA levels had insertions in piRNA clusters 38C or 42AB, where Rhino binding was largely Kipferl-independent (Figure 4D right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D.

claim: While piRNA levels from sub-telomeric TAS Satellites remained unchanged in kipferl-depleted ovaries, those derived from the Rsp and 1.688 Satellites increased strongly.
source: While piRNA levels from sub-telomeric TAS Satellites remained unchanged, those derived from the Rsp and 1.688 Satellites increased strongly in kipferl-depleted ovaries compared to control, consistent with increased Rhino occupancy at these loci (Figure 4E and F; Figure 3I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: Satellite piRNAs accounted for only 4% of all piRNAs in wildtype ovaries, but accounted for more than one in five piRNAs (21%) in kipferl-depleted ovaries.
source: As a result, Satellite piRNAs which accounted for only 4% of all piRNAs in wildtype ovaries, accounted for more than one in five piRNAs (21%) in kipferl-depleted ovaries.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the small RNA-seq analysis.

claim: The levels of poly-adenylated transcripts for a number of transposable elements increased significantly in kipferl-depleted ovaries.
source: The levels of poly-adenylated transcripts for a number of transposable elements increased significantly in kipferl-depleted ovaries (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is shown in the volcano plot in Figure 4G.

claim: RNA FISH experiments confirmed the de-repression of transposable elements in kipferl null mutant ovaries.
source: RNA FISH experiments confirmed the de-repression of these elements in kipferl null mutant ovaries (Figure 4H; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Transposon de-repression in ovaries lacking Kipferl was less severe compared to ovaries lacking Rhino.
source: In general, transposon de-repression in ovaries lacking Kipferl was less severe compared to ovaries lacking Rhino (Mohn et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on comparison with published data and the data in this manuscript.

claim: Loss of Kipferl had hardly any effect on overall gene expression, similar to the piRNA-specific factor Rhino.
source: Our combined genetic data suggested that Kipferl acts specifically in the piRNA pathway. Consistent with this, loss of Kipferl had hardly any effect on overall gene expression, similar to the piRNA-specific factor Rhino (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: In rhino mutant ovaries, Kipferl was distributed throughout nurse cell nuclei rather than being enriched in discrete nuclear foci as in wildtype ovaries.
source: In rhino mutant ovaries, Kipferl was distributed throughout nurse cell nuclei rather than being enriched in discrete nuclear foci as in wildtype ovaries (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Kipferl remained bound at most genomic 1-kb tiles that it occupied in wildtype ovaries in rhino mutant ovaries.
source: ChIP-seq experiments revealed that Kipferl nevertheless remained bound at most genomic 1-kb tiles that it occupied in wildtype ovaries (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Kipferl enrichment levels often differed between rhino-depleted and control ovaries, with a strong decrease observed at several regions, including the largely Kipferl-independent piRNA clusters 42AB and 38C.
source: Kipferl enrichment levels, however, often differed between rhino-depleted and control ovaries, with a strong decrease observed at several regions, including the largely Kipferl-independent piRNA clusters 42AB and 38C.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There is a strong interdependence of Rhino and Kipferl at regions they co-occupied in wildtype ovaries.
source: This revealed a strong interdependence of Rhino and Kipferl at regions they co-occupied in wildtype ovaries, which included most heterochromatic Kipferl binding sites, as well as roughly 60% of the euchromatic sites.

claim: Rhino's chromatin occupancy was highly dependent on Kipferl.
source: In agreement with our previous results, Rhino's chromatin occupancy was highly dependent on Kipferl.
evidence: This is demonstrated throughout the manuscript, particularly in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Loss of Rhino had a more complex effect on Kipferl's binding pattern: while the Kipferl ChIP-seq signal was reduced at sites co-occupied by Rhino, residual signal was visible at many of these loci.
source: Loss of Rhino had a more complex effect on Kipferl's binding pattern: while the Kipferl ChIP-seq signal was reduced at sites co-occupied by Rhino, residual signal was visible at many of these loci.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Kipferl binding at sites lacking Rhino enrichment was fully maintained in the absence of Rhino.
source: Furthermore, Kipferl binding at sites lacking Rhino enrichment was fully maintained in the absence of Rhino, supporting Kipferl's ability to bind to chromatin without Rhino.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: In rhino mutants, Kipferl was enriched at thousands of narrow peaks.
source: In rhino mutants, Kipferl was enriched at thousands of narrow peaks.
evidence: This is described in the text and shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: Kipferl's chromatin occupancy was reduced at sites that were co-occupied by Rhino in wildtype ovaries, while it was unaffected at Kipferl-only peaks in rhino mutants.
source: Comparison of the Kipferl signal between wildtype and rhino mutants at these sites confirmed that Kipferl's chromatin occupancy was reduced at sites that were co-occupied by Rhino in wildtype ovaries, while it was unaffected at Kipferl-only peaks (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claim: While Kipferl bound to chromatin in similarly narrow peaks at stand-alone and Rhino-occupied regions in rhino mutants, Rhino seemingly supported the spreading of Kipferl to larger domains in wildtype ovaries.
source: Moreover, while Kipferl bound to chromatin in similarly narrow peaks at stand-alone and Rhino-occupied regions in rhino mutants, Rhino seemingly supported the spreading of Kipferl to larger domains in wildtype ovaries.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and E.

claim: Kipferl binding sites in rhino mutants were found both in pericentromeric heterochromatin (802 peaks) and within chromosomal arms (3334 peaks).
source: Kipferl binding sites in rhino mutants were found both in pericentromeric heterochromatin (802 peaks) and within chromosomal arms (3334 peaks), and generally coincided with regions bound by Kipferl and Rhino in wildtype ovaries
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the ChIP-seq analysis.

claim: Kipferl's chromatin enrichment was strengthened and expanded from the narrow peaks seen in rhino mutant ovaries to broad domains in wildtype ovaries, specifically at peaks where Rhino was present.
source: Kipferl's chromatin enrichment was strengthened and expanded from the narrow peaks seen in rhino mutant ovaries to broad domains in wildtype ovaries, specifically at peaks where Rhino was present.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Kipferl peaks that did not show Rhino binding did not widen into extended domains.
source: Kipferl peaks that did not show Rhino binding, on the other hand, did not widen into extended domains.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Rhino recruitment to Kipferl peaks depended on the presence of H3K9me2/3: Rhino occupied the majority of Kipferl peaks in pericentromeric heterochromatin where H3K9me2/3 is abundant.
source: Importantly, Rhino recruitment to Kipferl peaks depended on the presence of H3K9me2/3: Rhino occupied the majority of Kipferl peaks in pericentromeric heterochromatin where H3K9me2/3 is abundant.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Within chromosomal arms, Rhino accumulated preferentially at those Kipferl sites that were within a local H3K9me2/3 domain.
source: Within chromosomal arms, Rhino accumulated preferentially at those Kipferl sites that were within a local H3K9me2/3 domain.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Rhino occupancy at and around Kipferl binding sites was dependent on Kipferl.
source: Consistent with this, Rhino occupancy at and around Kipferl binding sites was dependent on Kipferl
evidence: This is demonstrated throughout the manuscript, particularly in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Overexpression of Kipferl in germline cells resulted in increased Kipferl binding at all sites, leading to the strengthening of Rhino/Kipferl domains within H3K9me2/3 domains, and the formation of additional small Rhino domains at pre-existing Kipferl sites with low, but detectable H3K9me2/3 levels.
source: and overexpression of Kipferl in germline cells resulted in increased Kipferl binding at all sites, leading to the strengthening of Rhino/Kipferl domains within H3K9me2/3 domains, and the formation of additional small Rhino domains at pre-existing Kipferl sites with low, but detectable H3K9me2/3 levels (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Kipferl's intrinsic chromatin binding profile in rhino mutants was strongly predictive of Rhino's chromatin occupancy, often mirroring the non-uniform enrichment of Rhino in wildtype ovaries, only at lower levels.
source: Kipferl's intrinsic chromatin binding profile in rhino mutants was strongly predictive of Rhino's chromatin occupancy, often mirroring the non-uniform enrichment of Rhino in wildtype ovaries, only at lower levels (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F.

claim: 60% of Kipferl-dependent Rhino bound regions contained or were within 5 kb of a Kipferl nucleation site.
source: Indeed, 60% of Kipferl-dependent Rhino bound regions contained or were within 5 kb of a Kipferl nucleation site.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the ChIP-seq analysis.

claim: At several loci (e.g. the eyeless gene), the extended Rhino domain in wildtype flies encompassed only very weak or no putative Kipferl nucleation sites.
source: However, at several loci (e.g. the eyeless gene), the extended Rhino domain in wildtype flies encompassed only very weak or no putative Kipferl nucleation sites (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5G.

claim: In line with the largely Kipferl-independent Rhino occupancy at piRNA clusters 42AB and 38C, there is only weak intrinsic Kipferl binding at these loci.
source: Finally, in line with the largely Kipferl-independent Rhino occupancy at piRNA clusters 42AB and 38C, we find only weak intrinsic Kipferl binding at these loci (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Kipferl bound strongly to piRNA clusters 42AB and 38C in wildtype ovaries, implying that Rhino is capable of stabilizing Kipferl on chromatin.
source: Nevertheless, Kipferl bound strongly to these clusters in wildtype ovaries, implying that Rhino is capable of stabilizing Kipferl on chromatin.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5G and is an inference from the data.

claim: Kipferl influenced Rhino's chromatin profile even at the Kipferl-independent piRNA cluster 42AB: While Rhino remained bound at the highly repetitive central regions of this cluster in the absence of Kipferl, several small Kipferl nucleation sites towards the periphery of the cluster seem to support the formation of an extended Rhino domain in wildtype ovaries.
source: Upon closer inspection, Kipferl influenced Rhino's chromatin profile even at the Kipferl-independent piRNA cluster 42AB: While Rhino remained bound at the highly repetitive central regions of this cluster in the absence of Kipferl, several small Kipferl nucleation sites towards the periphery of the cluster seem to support the formation of an extended Rhino domain in wildtype ovaries (Figure 5G, zoom).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5G zoom panel.

claim: Kipferl is a major specificity factor for Rhino in ovaries.
source: Based on these data, we conclude that Kipferl is a major specificity factor for Rhino in ovaries
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Kipferl cooperates with Rhino to form extended Rhino domains from defined nucleation sites, with both proteins supporting each other's chromatin occupancy.
source: and that Kipferl cooperates with Rhino to form extended Rhino domains from defined nucleation sites, with both proteins supporting each other's chromatin occupancy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Kipferl is not the only Rhino specificity factor but is also required for the stabilization of Rhino domains nucleated by alternative means.
source: Our data further indicate that Kipferl is not the only Rhino specificity factor but demonstrate that it is also required for the stabilization of Rhino domains nucleated by alternative means.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data, particularly the observation of Kipferl-independent Rhino binding at clusters 42AB and 38C.

claim: Kipferl's two ZnF arrays are predicted to bind DNA with a specificity for guanosine-rich motifs.
source: According to the nucleation-site model, Kipferl is expected to bind to specific DNA motifs. Consistent with this, its two ZnF arrays are predicted to bind DNA with a specificity for guanosine-rich motifs (Figure 5H, Persikov and Singh, 2014).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5H and supported by the cited reference.

claim: The top enriched motif in Kipferl ChIP-seq peaks identified in rhino mutant ovaries was found in >80% of all peaks (p<10–322) and closely matched the in silico predictions for Kipferl's ZnF arrays.
source: We determined sequence motifs that were enriched in Kipferl ChIP-seq peaks identified in rhino mutant ovaries. The top enriched motif (found in >80% of all peaks; p<10–322) closely matched the in silico predictions for Kipferl's ZnF arrays (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The GRGGN motif was locally enriched at experimentally determined Kipferl peaks, regardless of whether the peak was located in pericentromeric heterochromatin or chromosomal arms, or whether it was within a Rhino domain or constituted a Kipferl-only site.
source: This GRGGN motif was locally enriched at experimentally determined Kipferl peaks, regardless of whether the peak was located in pericentromeric heterochromatin or chromosomal arms, or whether it was within a Rhino domain or constituted a Kipferl-only site (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Stable overexpression of FLAG-tagged Kipferl in cultured ovarian somatic stem cells (OSCs), which do not express Kipferl or Rhino, resulted in Kipferl binding at thousands of defined sites that were enriched in the GRGGN sequence motif.
source: In support of Kipferl's specificity for a GRGGN sequence, stable overexpression of FLAG-tagged Kipferl in cultured ovarian somatic stem cells (OSCs), which do not express Kipferl or Rhino, resulted in Kipferl binding at thousands of defined sites that were enriched in the GRGGN sequence motif (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: KipferlΔ1st-array showed strongly reduced chromatin binding capabilities.
source: KipferlΔ1st-array showed strongly reduced chromatin binding capabilities (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Deletion of the second ZnF array (KipferlΔ2nd-array) had only mild impacts on chromatin binding.
source: Deletion of the second ZnF array (KipferlΔ2nd-array) instead had only mild impacts.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The N-terminal ZAD promotes anti-parallel homodimerization.
source: The N-terminal ZAD, which is characteristic for the >90 ZAD-ZnF family members in D. melanogaster, promotes anti-parallel homodimerization but has not been directly linked to DNA binding (Jauch et al., 2003; Bonchuk et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Yeast two-hybrid experiments confirmed the dimerization capability of Kipferl's ZAD.
source: Yeast two-hybrid experiments confirmed the dimerization capability of Kipferl's ZAD (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Deletion of the ZAD resulted in a global loss of Kipferl ChIP-seq signal.
source: Deletion of the ZAD, and therefore abrogation of Kipferl dimerization, resulted in a global loss of Kipferl ChIP-seq signal (Figure 6B)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Kipferl binds chromatin as a dimer, primarily via its first ZnF array.
source: Together, these findings indicated that Kipferl binds chromatin as a dimer, primarily via its first ZnF array.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 6B.

claim: Yeast two-hybrid experiments confirmed that Rhino interacts with Kipferl's first ZnF array, with no additional interaction interfaces being identified.
source: Yeast two-hybrid experiments, probing full length Rhino against Kipferl fragments, confirmed that Rhino interacts with Kipferl's first ZnF array, with no additional interaction interfaces being identified (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The 4th ZnF (ZnF#4) of Kipferl plays a critical role in the interaction between Rhino and Kipferl.
source: To disentangle the putative DNA-binding and Rhino-binding activities of the first ZnF array, we further narrowed down the interaction between Rhino and Kipferl, revealing a critical role of the 4th ZnF (ZnF#4, Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: In flies expressing KipferlΔZnF#4 instead of the endogenous protein, Rhino did not co-localize with Kipferl, and displayed the characteristic kipferl mutant phenotype.
source: In flies expressing KipferlΔZnF#4 instead of the endogenous protein, Rhino did not co-localize with Kipferl, and displayed the characteristic kipferl mutant phenotype (Figure 6D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Rhino lost its chromatin occupancy in kipferlΔZnF#4 flies in a pattern also seen in kipferl null mutants.
source: Moreover, Rhino lost its chromatin occupancy in kipferlΔZnF#4 flies in a pattern also seen in kipferl null mutants (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6E.

claim: kipferlΔZnF#4 females were sub-fertile.
source: KipferlΔZnF#4 was diffusely localized in nurse cell nuclei akin to wildtype Kipferl in rhino mutants, and kipferlΔZnF#4 females were sub-fertile (Figure 6D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: KipferlΔZnF#4 retained full chromatin binding ability as it was enriched at Kipferl binding sites in a pattern closely mirroring that of wildtype Kipferl in a rhino mutant.
source: Strikingly, KipferlΔZnF#4 retained full chromatin binding ability as it was enriched at Kipferl binding sites in a pattern closely mirroring that of wildtype Kipferl in a rhino mutant (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The Rhino- and chromatin-binding activities of Kipferl can be uncoupled: ZnFs 1–3, supplemented by the second ZnF array, allow for putative sequence specific DNA binding, while ZnF 4 interacts with Rhino.
source: The Rhino- and chromatin-binding activities of Kipferl can therefore be uncoupled: ZnFs 1–3, supplemented by the second ZnF array, allow for putative sequence specific DNA binding, while ZnF 4 interacts with Rhino.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 6.

claim: Kipferl interacts with Rhino's chromodomain.
source: We inverted the yeast two-hybrid assay to determine which region of Rhino interacts with Kipferl and discovered that Kipferl interacts with Rhino's chromodomain (Figure 6H; Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Kipferl did not interact with the Rhino chromoshadow domain, the Rhino hinge region, or the chromodomain of Su(var)2–5.
source: Kipferl did not interact with the Rhino chromoshadow domain, the Rhino hinge region, or the chromodomain of Su(var)2–5.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Both RhinoCSD-Gcn4 and Rhinoart.-hinge failed to form extended Rhino domains like the wildtype protein, but were enriched at prominent Kipferl nucleation sites such as those in cluster 80F or upstream of the headcase gene.
source: To test these findings in vivo, we generated flies that expressed Rhino variants with an artificial hinge or with a Gcn4 dimerization domain instead of the chromoshadow domain. Both RhinoCSD-Gcn4 and Rhinoart.-hinge failed to form extended Rhino domains like the wildtype protein, but were enriched at prominent Kipferl nucleation sites such as those in cluster 80F or upstream of the headcase gene (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Transposon sequences overall do not harbor more GRGGN motif occurrences than random genomic tiles.
source: In fact, transposon sequences overall do not harbor more GRGGN motif occurrences than random genomic tiles (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There is a large spread of motif density among transposons.
source: Instead, we observed a large spread of motif density among transposons (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The GC-rich gypsy8 and Rt1a/b/c elements harbored between 29 and 38 GRGGN motifs, while the AT-rich Rsp and 1.688 Satellites harbored none.
source: The GC-rich gypsy8 and Rt1a/b/c elements harbored between 29 and 38 motifs, while the AT-rich Rsp and 1.688 Satellites harbored none (Figure 7A; Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Motif density per kilobase showed a significant correlation with Kipferl's intrinsic ability to bind to transposon sequences (R=0.64, p<2.2e-16).
source: Motif density per kilobase showed a significant correlation with Kipferl's intrinsic ability to bind to transposon sequences (as measured by Kipferl ChIP-seq enrichment in rhino mutant ovaries; R=0.64, p<2.2e-16) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B.

claim: For most elements, the extent of Rhino-independent Kipferl enrichment was directly correlated with their respective Rhino enrichment levels in wildtype ovaries (R=0.83, p<2.2e-16).
source: For most elements, the extent of Rhino-independent Kipferl enrichment was moreover directly correlated with their respective Rhino enrichment levels in wildtype ovaries (Figure 7A and C; R=0.83, p<2.2e-16).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A and C.

claim: Exceptions to the correlation between Kipferl and Rhino enrichment were telomeric transposons and a few elements contained in clusters 42AB or 38C; these transposons were occupied by Rhino in wildtype ovaries despite no baseline Kipferl binding, and they maintained Rhino binding in kipferl-depleted ovaries.
source: Exceptions were telomeric transposons and a few elements contained in clusters 42AB or 38C; these transposons were occupied by Rhino in wildtype ovaries despite no baseline Kipferl binding, and they maintained Rhino binding in kipferl-depleted ovaries, supporting the previous notion that Kipferl-independent chromatin recruitment mechanisms for Rhino likely exist (Figure 7C; Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The occurrence of the guanosine-rich Kipferl motif correlated with overall GC-content.
source: As the occurrence of the guanosine-rich Kipferl motif correlated with overall GC-content, enrichments for both Kipferl and Rhino on transposons also correlated with the elements GC-content (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, E, F; Rmotif-GC=0.78, p<2.2e-16; RGC-Kipf=0.71, p<2.2e-16; RGC-Rhi=0.59, p<1.1e-13).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, E, F.

claim: The correlation between GC-content and Rhino enrichment was abolished in ovaries depleted for Kipferl, indicating that Rhino's preferential binding to GC-rich transposons is due to Kipferl-mediated recruitment and/or stabilization of Rhino on DNA sequences with Kipferl motifs.
source: The correlation between GC-content and Rhino enrichment was abolished in ovaries depleted for Kipferl, indicating that Rhino's preferential binding to GC-rich transposons is due to Kipferl-mediated recruitment and/or stabilization of Rhino on DNA sequences with Kipferl motifs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G, R = 0.08, p=0.34).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1G.

claim: A combination of Kipferl and Piwi-dependent H3K9me2/3 is required to stabilize Rhino even on those transposons that do not contain strong Kipferl nucleation sites.
source: We conclude that a combination of Kipferl and Piwi-dependent H3K9me2/3 is required to stabilize Rhino even on those transposons that do not contain strong Kipferl nucleation sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 7D.

claim: Kipferl supports Rhino at stand-alone transposon insertions in one of two ways: In some instances, Rhino-bound insertions occurred nearby a genomic Kipferl binding site, which might be a critical factor to establish a local Rhino domain. In other instances, there is no nearby Kipferl binding site, and Kipferl likely acts by stabilizing Rhino which might have been recruited through alternative nucleation factors.
source: Based on manual inspection of individual transposon insertions in the different examined fly strains (illustrated in Figure 7E), we propose that Kipferl supports Rhino at stand-alone transposon insertions in one of two ways. In some instances, we find that Rhino-bound insertions occurred nearby a genomic Kipferl binding site, which might be a critical factor to establish a local Rhino domain. In other instances, we find no nearby Kipferl binding site. Here, Kipferl likely acts by stabilizing Rhino which might have been recruited through alternative nucleation factors akin to Kipferl's role at piRNA clusters 38C and 42AB, where Rhino remains chromatin bound in Kipferl mutant ovaries.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 7E and is a model based on the data.

claim: Kipferl acts as a recruitment factor for Rhino, and it stabilizes the formation of extended Rhino domains, both at its own recruitment sites and at domains nucleated by alternative specificity factors.
source: Taken altogether, our data indicate that Kipferl acts as a recruitment factor for Rhino, and that it stabilizes the formation of extended Rhino domains, both at its own recruitment sites and at domains nucleated by alternative specificity factors.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The discovery of Kipferl critically advances our understanding of how dual-strand piRNA source loci are specified.
source: This study provides direct evidence that DNA sequence is an important determinant of how germline cells define the chromatin binding sites of the fast-evolving HP1 variant protein Rhino. The discovery of Kipferl, a putative DNA-binding zinc finger protein, that cooperates with the H3K9me3 chromatin mark and serves as Rhino guidance factor critically advances our understanding of how dual-strand piRNA source loci are specified.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's contribution.

claim: Rhino is among the fastest evolving proteins in the fly genome.
source: Intriguingly, Rhino is among the fastest evolving proteins in the fly genome (Vermaak et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Kipferl is conserved among Drosophila species with stronger divergence outside the melanogaster clade.
source: Kipferl is conserved among Drosophila species with stronger divergence outside the melanogaster clade.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The X-chromosomal 1.688 Satellite array (359 bp repeat) spans more than 10 Mbp on the pericentromeric X-chromosome and acts as a hybrid lethality locus in crosses between D. melanogaster and D. simulans.
source: The largest 1.688 Satellite array, the X-chromosomal 359 bp repeat, spans more than 10 Mbp on the pericentromeric X-chromosome and acts as a hybrid lethality locus in crosses between D. melanogaster and D. simulans (Ferree and Barbash, 2009; Chen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Females lacking the 1.688 repeat, when mated to wildtype males, generate non-viable offspring while no defects occur in the reciprocal cross.
source: Females lacking this repeat, when mated to wildtype males, generate non-viable offspring while no defects occur in the reciprocal cross.
evidence: This is a documented genetic phenomenon.

claim: The Rsp Satellite has been identified genetically as part of the Segregation Distorter system, a meiotic drive system in males.
source: The Rsp Satellite has been identified genetically as part of the Segregation Distorter system, a meiotic drive system in males (Larracuente and Presgraves, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Both Rsp and 1.688 Satellites give rise to abundant piRNAs in a Rhino-dependent manner in testes and ovaries.
source: Both Rsp and 1.688 Satellites give rise to abundant piRNAs in a Rhino-dependent manner in testes and ovaries (Wei et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.
